title: Invest in Your Future
blurb: Talk about future plans and predictions

steps.html:
Auto transport analyst. Garbage designer. Nostalgist. A careers consultant describes jobs that do not exist yet, and two students decide what they think of them.

  • Follow a radio interview about the future of work
  • Choose between will, going to and the present continuous
  • Talk about intentions, plans and predictions
  • Write about your own plans for the next five years

steps.title: Language noticing.
steps.sub: The student says: 'I graduate this summer' and 'It's probably going to be quite hard to get a job.'
steps.prompt: Why are the two forms different?
options: The first is fixed by the university timetable; the second is a prediction based on what she can see now.
The first is a prediction; the second is a fixed arrangement.
There is no difference — either form would work in both.
steps.answer: The first is fixed by the university timetable; the second is a prediction based on what she can see now.
steps.why: A timetabled event takes the present simple. A prediction based on present evidence takes going to. This is the rule you will study next.

steps.title: Read between the lines.
steps.sub: The text describes people who recreate a past decade in detail, and does so without mockery.
steps.prompt: What position is the writer taking?
options: That the hobby is eccentric and should be explained rather than judged.
That the past was in fact better than the present.
steps.answer: That the hobby is eccentric and should be explained rather than judged.
steps.why: The absence of mockery is itself the position. The writer is describing what the enthusiasm is for, not endorsing the preference.

steps.title: will, going to, the present continuous, the present simple
steps.html:
Four forms, four different jobs. The complete rule, then a large example bank.

English has no future tense. It has several present forms doing future work, and the choice says how the future thing is connected to now.

will — a prediction or an opinion about the future, with nothing arranged; also a decision made at the moment of speaking. Trains probably won't have drivers. I think I'll be an auto transport analyst.

going to — an intention already formed, or a prediction based on evidence you can see now. I'm going to work in design. It's going to be quite hard to get a job.

present continuous — a fixed arrangement, usually with another person and usually with a time or place attached. I'm meeting the careers adviser on Thursday.

present simple — a timetable or a schedule that is not yours to change. I graduate this summer. The train leaves at six.

The frequent error at B2 is using will for arrangements: I will meet him on Thursday when the meeting is already fixed. Use the present continuous.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Twelve sentences from the interview.

The world of work will naturally change with it.
A prediction.

There will probably be more jobs in healthcare.
Probably sits after will.

Trains and buses probably won't have drivers any more.
Negative prediction; probably before won't.

We'll have self-driving vehicles.
Prediction, contracted.

I don't think we'll see them as specific skills.
The negative goes on think, not on will.

I think I'll be an auto transport analyst.
A decision, or a joke, made at the moment of speaking.

IT skills are going to be vital.
A prediction the speaker is confident about.

I'm certainly going to work in design in some way.
An intention already formed.

I'm studying design.
Present continuous, but about now — not the future.

I graduate this summer.
Present simple: the university's timetable.

It's probably going to be quite hard to get a job.
Prediction from present evidence: high unemployment.

Let me know if you do decide to become a nostalgist.
After if, use the present, not will.

steps.title: Four sentences about the same afternoon
steps.html:
1. The facts: your course finishes at four; you have already agreed to meet a careers adviser at half past; you have decided to apply for a job in design; and you think you will not get it.
  2. The course finishing is a timetable, not yours to change: My course finishes at four. Present simple.
  3. The meeting is a fixed arrangement with another person: I'm seeing the careers adviser at half past. Present continuous.
  4. Applying is an intention you have already formed: I'm going to apply for a job in design.
  5. Not getting it is a prediction with nothing arranged: I probably won't get it. Four futures, one afternoon.

steps.title: You are going to write about your own next five years.
steps.sub: Which will you build it around?

options.label: A skill you intend to learn

steps.title: Write your plan.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Include at least one fixed arrangement, one intention, one prediction and one timetabled event.
steps.html:
• Open with something already timetabled — a date you cannot change.
  • Add one fixed arrangement, in the present continuous.
  • State one intention, with <i>going to</i>.
  • Make one prediction, with <i>will</i> or <i>probably won't</i>.
  • Close with what you genuinely do not know.

Useful language

  • I finish / the course starts … (timetable)
  • I'm meeting … next week. (arrangement)
  • I'm going to … (intention)
  • I think I'll probably … (prediction)
  • It's going to be hard to … , because …
  • Moreover, …
steps.modelHtml:
The next five years

My contract finishes in June, which is the one date I cannot move. I'm meeting my old supervisor next Thursday to ask whether the research post is still open, and I will know more after that.

Whatever she says, I'm going to apply for the master's. I've thought about it for two years and I have stopped finding reasons not to. It is going to be expensive, and I will probably have to keep working two days a week to pay for it.

After that I honestly do not know. I think I'll stay in the city for another five years at least; my sister is here and the work is here. Moreover, everybody I know who left came back within eighteen months, which tells me something.
